summary: A 1970 note on an official protocol mechanism, by Steve Crocker. It concerns how protocols would be formally put forward within the group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 53 describes how the Network Working Group planned to create and revise an official Host-Host protocol. It sets out a proposal, community review, and ARPA approval process.

subtitle: A six-step process for proposing and approving the official Host-Host protocol.

tldr.problem: The network community needed a process for establishing and changing an official Host-Host protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Proposals are circulated as NWG/RFCs, reviewed by the community before a cutoff date, and sent to the ARPA office for approval if substantially accepted.
tldr.outcome: The note records decisions from a discussion at the Spring Joint Computer Conference and says the first official protocol would be proposed that month.

sections.title: Decisions on Protocol Governance
sections.content:
During the Spring Joint Computer Conference in Atlantic City, Larry Roberts, Barry Wessler, Cordell Green, Jon Postel, and Steve Crocker discussed rules for establishing and modifying an official Host-Host protocol.

RFC 53 records six decisions about documentation, proposal development, community comments, and approval.
sections.plainLanguage: The participants agreed on a process for publishing and reviewing proposals for the official Host-Host protocol. This memo records those decisions.

sections.title: Proposal, Review, and Approval
sections.content:
A new set of documents would specify the official protocol and be maintained at the Network Information Center when appropriate. Steve Crocker would distribute proposals for the initial protocol and later changes as NWG/RFCs, using suggestions from interested parties.

Each proposal would include a cutoff date for community feedback. If substantial criticism emerged, the process would stop without changing the official protocol. If the proposal was substantially accepted, it and minor revisions would go to the ARPA office for approval or disapproval.
sections.plainLanguage: Interested parties could suggest changes, and the community could comment by a stated deadline. Accepted proposals still needed approval from the ARPA office.

sections.title: After Approval
sections.content: After ARPA approval, Crocker would distribute the new protocol. The note states that the first version of an official protocol would be offered that month.
sections.plainLanguage: Once approved, the new protocol would be distributed. The note expected the first version to be proposed in June 1970.
